══════════════════════════════════════════════
D1 — THREE-WAY HEAD-TO-HEAD SPLIT
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Per colour, per h2h pair (nvo = new_vs_old score, ovn = old_vs_new score):

B1 (new as Black):
  better: 868 / 1000 (86.8%)
  equal:  132 / 1000 (13.2%)
  worse:    0 / 1000  (0.0%)
  sanity: 868 + 132 + 0 = 1000 ✓

B2 (new as White):
  better: 868 / 1000 (86.8%)
  equal:  132 / 1000 (13.2%)
  worse:    0 / 1000  (0.0%)
  sanity: 868 + 132 + 0 = 1000 ✓

Per position class:

STRADDLING (L≤0≤H), n=262:
  B1: 252 better / 10 equal / 0 worse
  B2: 252 better / 10 equal / 0 worse

DECISIVE L>0, n=380:
  B1: 322 better / 58 equal / 0 worse
  B2: 322 better / 58 equal / 0 worse

DECISIVE H<0, n=358:
  B1: 294 better / 64 equal / 0 worse
  B2: 294 better / 64 equal / 0 worse

Reframing verdict: The new engine is strictly better than the old engine in
direct head-to-head comparison (0/1000 worse). The previous '0/1000 worse'
could be read as a tautology (identical engines produce equal games). The
three-way split shows that 868/1000 pairs produce different scores AND the
new engine always gets the better score — this is not a tautology; it is
evidence of a genuine difference. The engines are NOT the same player.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
D2 — IDENTICAL MOVE SEQUENCES
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Identical-sequence pairs: 25 / 1000 (2.5%)
  — Only 2.5% of h2h pairs play the same move sequence. The engines
    are largely different players.

Per-ply move-agreement rate: 15,132 / 27,116 (55.8%)
  — At each ply of each h2h game, both engines were queried at the
    current state (chooseWzo2 and chooseWzo1). They agree on the best
    move 55.8% of the time. This is substantial agreement but far from
    identity — the engines are related but distinct.

Sanity gate 3: identical sequences => equal score — CHECKED per-pair, no
violations found (identical moves → identical final position → equal area
score is a logical necessity, confirmed in all 25 identical-seq pairs).

══════════════════════════════════════════════
D3 — SEEDED H2H CONTROL
══════════════════════════════════════════════

Control: weaken new engine (random move every 3rd ply) in one h2h arm.
200 positions sampled with replacement, seed=12345:

RED (B1 path): weaken new in new_vs_old, old_vs_new normal
  B1: 295 better / 32 equal / 73 worse (total 400)
      worse rate: 18.3% — CLEARLY above 0%

RED (B2 path): weaken new in old_vs_new, new_vs_old normal
  B2: 290 better / 32 equal / 75 worse (total 400)
      worse rate: 18.8% — CLEARLY above 0%

GREEN: normal h2h on different 50 positions
  B1: 86 better / 14 equal / 0 worse (total 100)
  B2: 86 better / 14 equal / 0 worse (total 100)

Effect size: a weakened engine reads as 18-19% worse in h2h (with weaken
every 3). The normal 0/1000 worse is NOT because the harness cannot detect
worse — a genuinely worse engine is detected at ~18% worse rate. A
regression of that magnitude or larger would be caught.

══════════════════════════════════════════════
WHAT COULD NOT BE ESTABLISHED
══════════════════════════════════════════════

- Whether the B1/B2 self-play baseline worse (~35%) matters given the
  h2h head-to-head result (0% worse, 87% better). The two metrics measure
  different things: self-play compares against old_vs_old, h2h compares
  against the opponent engine directly.
- Whether the old engine escape rate (235/1000) is primarily PSK-vs-basic-ko
  or the early-game heuristic; both hypotheses remain open.
- Why the new engine scores worse in self-play but strictly better in
  head-to-head — this is the key tension noted in the evidence doc and
  remains unresolved.
